newsitem.title: USA: High school students finance skills badly lacking.
newsitem.headline: High school students finance skills badly lacking.

text.p: Most high school seniors fail to make the grade when it comes to their personal finance know-how, according to a national survey released on Thursday.
On average, students across the country gave the right answers to just 57 percent of 31 survey questions -- a failing grade based on the traditional scale used by schools.

"The results are not very hopeful," said Lewis Mandell, dean of business at Marquette University, who conducted the survey for the JumpStart Coalition, a group of federal agencies, universities and non-profit organisations.
Only 5 percent of respondents earned a "C" grade -- the minimum grade average required to graduate from most colleges -- by giving the right answers to 75 percent or more questions.
"Ninety-five percent of our students are incapable of graduating to be able to play at the game of life," Mandell said.

The findings, drawn from more than 1,500 students at 64 high schools nationwide, showed students knew the least about the area of savings and investments. Students answered only 47.3 percent of the questions in that category correctly.
A mere 14 percent correctly said that stocks would likely have a higher growth rate over 18 years than savings accounts, checking accounts or government savings bonds.

Mandell noted the dire consequences of the students' lack of knowledge about the stock market's ability to outperform traditional savings vehicles over time, given the increased responsibility individuals must take in saving for retirement.
The group found that females, who answered 57.8 percent of the questions correctly, averaged slightly higher scores than males, who got 56.7 percent.
The average score for Caucasian students was 60.7 percent, compared with 55.7 for Asians, 55.1 for Hispanics, 50.3 percent for African-Americans and 48.8 percent for Native Americans.
But scores were not dependent on family income, the survey found.

Average scores were slightly lower for students in the over $80,000 a year income bracket than for those in the bracket just below, suggesting the most affluent students were insulated from financial worries, the group said.
But the 2 percent of students who had no education plans beyond high school scored far lower, answering just 43.8 percent of the survey questions correctly.
More than half of the students said that a certificate of deposit at a bank is not protected against loss by the federal government.

The coalition, which includes representatives from the Federal Reserve and the securities industry, said it will use the survey results to revise a set of guidelines it has developed to help schools teach personal finance.

The coalition's executive director, Dara Duguay, acknowledged that many adults appear unable to manage their finances, judging by the marked rise in personal bankruptcies and consumer credit delinquencies.
In some cases, "parents don't know how to help themselves much less their children," Duquay said at a press conference.
